title: The Memory Palace
tagline: A banquet, a falling roof and the poet who remembered where everyone sat. The oldest method of all, and the one that holds a hundred things.
card: The story of Simonides and the banquet, and how to turn a building you know into a memory with as many places as you need.
goal: you will learn the method of loci: choose a building, fix a route, pick distinct places along it, and use them to store a list in order.

left_off.q: How many pegs does the body system have, and in what order do they run?
left_off.a: Ten: head, eyes, nose, mouth, neck, chest, stomach, legs, feet, toes.

left_off.q: Why does a picture need to touch or act on the peg?
left_off.a: So you feel it there; the interaction is what fixes the picture to the place.

left_off.q: What is the limit of body pegs?
left_off.a: About ten; more places would be crowded or hard to tell apart.

story.heading: The banquet and the falling roof

text: Greece, over two thousand years ago. A rich nobleman named Scopas gave a great banquet in his house in Thessaly. Among the guests was the poet Simonides of Ceos, who had been paid to perform a poem in honour of his host. The poem, as poets did in those days, also praised the twin gods Castor and Pollux.

Scopas was not pleased. He said, in front of his guests, that he would pay only half the fee for the poem about himself. The rest, he said, could be collected from the twins. And he turned back to his wine.

check.q: Why was Scopas angry with Simonides?
check.a: The poet had spent part of the poem praising the twin gods Castor and Pollux, so Scopas said he would pay for only half and that the gods could pay the rest.

parts.talk: Have you ever been paid less than you were promised? What did you do?

text: A little later a servant came to the poet and said that two young men were waiting outside and wanted to see him urgently. Simonides went to the door. There was no one there.

At that very moment the roof of the banqueting hall fell in. Scopas and the guests were crushed. When the families arrived they could not recognise their dead: the bodies were beyond identifying. And so Simonides was asked, 'Who was sitting where?'

check.a: He was called outside by two young men who then were not there. The roof fell while he was out.

parts.talk: In the old story the twin gods were the young men outside. Why do you think the story was told that way?

text: Simonides closed his eyes, and he could see the hall again. He could see where each guest had been sitting: the old man by the window, the merchant on the left of the host, the pair of brothers near the door. He walked from place to place in his mind and named the people one by one, and the families could bury their own.

The story comes to us from the Roman writer Cicero, who tells it as the origin of the art of memory. We cannot know if it happened. But the lesson Cicero draws is clear and true: order is what makes a memory, and the best order is a place. If you can walk through a place, you can walk through a list.

check.q: What does the story teach about memory?
check.a: Remembering where things are, in a place we know, lets us recall them in order. Order and place are the key.

parts.talk: Think of a building you know well. Could you walk through it in your head with your eyes shut? What would you see first?

image.alt: An engraving of a banquet hall just after the roof has fallen in, with small gold stars marking where each guest sat and one lone figure in the doorway with a lantern.
image.cap: the hall after the roof fell: gold stars where each guest sat

words.m: Latin for 'a place'. A locus is one spot in your palace where you put a picture.
another word for a locus: a place you stop on your route.
the path you follow through your palace, the same every time.
to press something so hard that it is broken. The roof crushed the guests.
to say who or what someone or something is. She could not identify the body.
clearly different from the others. Each room should look distinct.

source: The story is told by Cicero in De Oratore II. It is a famous founding legend, not a verified event. Retold in our own words.
method_heading: Building a palace, step by step

method.x: A memory palace is a real place you know very well, with a fixed route through it. Along the route you choose places, and in each place you put one vivid picture. This is the method of loci.

data.label: A plan of a small house with a route of six numbered places

method.cap: The dashed route never changes. Walk it the same way every time.

items.h: Choose a place you know very well.
items.x: Your home, a house you grew up in, your school, a street you walk every day. Real beats invented, because you already know it.

items.h: Fix a route and never change it.
items.x: Start at a door and walk through the rooms in a single direction. The route gives the list its order.
A door, a sofa, a window, a stove. Each should be clearly different from its neighbours and not too close to them. Five to ten in a room is plenty.

items.h: Put one vivid picture at each place.
items.x: On it, in it or through it. Use what you learned in rooms 2 and 3: movement, size, senses.
Go through the places in order and look at each one. The picture will be there.

method.title: One item in one place
method.given: Palace: your home. Place 1: the front door. Item: PIZZA.
lines: A giant pizza covers the whole door.
Melted cheese drips down the steps; the door sticks to the pizza when you try to open it.
It sizzles and the smell makes you dizzy.
method.pic: You arrive at your front door and find it covered by a steaming pizza the size of a bed. The door is stuck to it and you can hear it sizzle.

items: Choose places that are well lit and not crowded.
Keep the places a moderate distance apart. Too close and they blur; too far and the walk is long.
Make each place distinct. Two identical armchairs are a trap.
Real is better than invented, because you do not have to learn the building as well as the list.

method.x:
place + picture
+ the same route
= recall.

A house with ten rooms and five places in each holds fifty items. A second house gives you fifty more. Memory champions use many palaces. In room 24 you will learn how to link several together. For now, one house and about ten places is plenty.
Describe the route through your first palace aloud, naming each of your first six places in order.

try.title: Choose your first palace
try.prompt: Write the name of a place you know very well, and list the first ten places on your route in order. Door, sofa, window and so on. Make sure each one is different.
try.model: For example: My grandmother's flat. 1 front door, 2 coat hooks, 3 hall mirror, 4 kitchen table, 5 stove, 6 fridge, 7 living-room sofa, 8 window, 9 bookcase, 10 bedroom bed. Each is a different object, in a fixed order.
checks: I know this place very well.
I have ten places in a fixed order.
No two of my places look alike.

try.title: Put one item in your first place
try.prompt: Your first place is where your route starts. Put a motorcycle there. Use size, colour, movement and senses.
try.model: A bright red motorcycle, the size of a bus, is crashing through the front door, roaring and sending sparks across the hall. Its engine shakes the walls and the smell of petrol is everywhere.
checks: The picture is at the first place on my route.
It uses at least one sense besides sight.

try.title: Three items in three places
try.prompt: Place a pizza at place 1, an elephant at place 2 and an explosion at place 3 of your palace. Write the three pictures.
try.model: 1: A giant pizza covers the front door, steaming and sticky. 2: An elephant is standing on the coat hooks, spraying water over the coats. 3: A huge silent explosion of confetti bursts out of the hall mirror.
checks: Each picture sits at its place.
Each picture is different from the others.
Each moves or makes a sound.

try.q: Which of these makes the best locus in a palace?
opts: The third of five identical chairs in a row
A distinctive stove in the kitchen
A very dark corner you have never looked at properly
try.why: A clear, distinct, well-lit object that you know well. Identical items blur together and dark or unknown places are hard to see.

items.s: A memory palace is a real place you know well, with a ___ route that never changes.
A single place in the palace where you put a picture is called a ___.

try.title: The walk, aloud
try.prompt: Walk your route aloud, naming each of your ten places in order, and say what you will put first at place 1, 2 and 3.

cards: Memory technique: pictures placed at distinct places along a fixed route in a familiar place.
One place in the palace where you put a picture. Plural: loci.
The path through the palace. Fixed: never changed, so it gives the order.
Distinct, well lit, not crowded, a moderate distance from the next one.
The poet who, in the legend, named the dead guests by remembering where each sat.
Walk the route and look at each place; the picture is waiting.
As many places as you can find. A house holds dozens; many houses hold hundreds.

quiz.q: Why does the route have to be fixed?
opts: It gives the list its order
quiz.why: The sequence of places becomes the sequence of items.

opts: A grand castle you saw once on holiday
The house you lived in for ten years
A made-up castle with a hundred rooms
quiz.why: A place you know well costs nothing to remember. The other two have to be learned.

quiz.q: How many items can a palace hold?
opts: As many places as it has, and you can add more palaces
quiz.why: As many as you have distinct places for.

quiz.q: What should you do if two of your places look very similar?
quiz.why: Similar places get mixed up; choose distinct ones.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: the first ten Roman emperors
challenge.intro: Put the first ten emperors of Rome into the first ten places of your palace, in order. Hint: use sound-alikes. Augustus = August sun; Tiberius = tyre; Caligula = call a goalie; Claudius = clouds; Nero = near-O (or Nero fiddling); Galba = gal with a bar; Otho = other; Vitellius = vital; Vespasian = a Vespa scooter; Titus = tight.
challenge.study: Walk your route in your head. One picture per place, in order.

look_back.q: What are the first five body pegs?
Name four tools from SMASHIN' SCOPE.
look_back.a: For example: Movement, Humour, Colour, Exaggeration, Number, Symbolism, Senses.

look_back.q: What do the words encoding, storage and retrieval name?
look_back.a: The three stages of memory: taking in, keeping, and getting back out.

look_back.q: Why does the body only hold about ten items?
look_back.a: There are only ten distinct, ordered places that are easy to tell apart. A palace has many more.

can_do: explain how Simonides's story teaches order and place.
choose a good palace and fix a route through it.
put a list of ten items into ten loci and recall them in order.
reflect: Which building do you know best? Walk through it in your head for a minute: where would your route begin, and which three places would you use first?
